A customer asks for a refund but leaves out the order number. Who decides what to do next?

A model can draft a reply for a person to send. Give it a choice of actions, and it can ask to look up the order, read the result, and use what it learns to pick its next step. The part that proposes each step is the **policy**. The software around it, the **runtime**, checks what is allowed, carries out approved actions, and decides when to stop.

::: {.callout-note}
## Where this block fits

This course builds **AutoResearch**, an agent that chooses machine-learning experiments. In this block you design its first loop. The model suggests what to try, the runtime checks the budget, and the result helps the model choose the next experiment. Later blocks build on that loop. The [case study](../case-studies/autoresearch.qmd#building-autoresearch-block-by-block) shows what each block adds.
:::

Start with the refund ticket. Once you can point to who chose each step, follow the same decisions through one AutoResearch experiment.

## Learning objectives

- Trace who picks the next step in a single LLM call, a fixed pipeline, a rules workflow, a learned router, and an agent.
- Distinguish what happened, what the runtime recorded, and what the model saw.
- Read one turn of an agent loop in plain language and in the notation used for sequential decisions.
- Explain what a bounded agent adds over a fixed workflow and how to measure whether the additional control is worth deploying.
- Explain who proposes an experiment, who approves it, how a winner is chosen, and when the search ends.

## 1. From answers to actions

People use “agent” for systems as different as a chatbot that routes a request and a coding assistant that works through a series of failed tests. Anthropic and OpenAI both emphasize who directs the work when describing their designs [@anthropic2024effectiveagents; @openaindbuildingagents].

Try this test. Keep the ticket and the rules the same. If the model gave a different valid answer, could it send the ticket down a different path? If so, the model controls a decision. Next ask whether it gets another choice after it sees the result.

### Who picks the next step

A customer's blender arrived cracked. They want a refund, but their account has two orders and the ticket gives no order number. The support team can refund the order, pass the case to a person, or reject the request. Refunds above \$100 or for orders older than 30 days require human review. As you follow @fig-agent-control-progression, watch who decides to look up the missing order.

::: {#fig-agent-control-progression}

```{=html}

{{< include _figures/design-comparison.html >}}

```

One support ticket, five designs (schematic example). What changes is who picks the next step. Cost, latency, and risk follow from that choice.

:::

Each row gives the model a different job.

- **Single LLM call.** The model drafts a reply. A person decides what to do with it.
- **Fixed pipeline.** The model summarizes the ticket, labels it, and drafts a reply. Code sets that order for every ticket.
- **Rules workflow.** The model extracts the item and order number. Code sends this ticket to a person because the number is missing. The extracted details still need checking. An invented order number could send the ticket down the wrong path.
- **Learned router.** The model chooses the refund handler. The handler needs an order number, so code sends the case to a person. The model gets one choice.
- **Agent.** The model asks to see the orders. After the lookup identifies the blender, the model proposes refunding order #1043. It gets to choose again with evidence it lacked on the first turn.

The pipeline, rules workflow, and router all follow a process laid out in code [@anthropic2024effectiveagents]. The pipeline follows a fixed sequence. The rules workflow branches on an extracted detail. The router lets the model pick the branch once.

Imagine the lookup had returned a price of \$140 for the blender. The model could then ask a person to review the case. What the model learns from one step can change what it chooses next. That is a **feedback-conditioned decision**. The sequence of steps it helps shape is the **trajectory**.

On this ticket the agent saves a person time. It also uses two extra model calls and a lookup, and it could choose the wrong order. The \$100 and 30-day rule checks price and age. Two different orders could both pass those checks.

### The control boundary

Look at the order lookup itself. A developer could write a rule that always looks up orders when the number is missing. Or the model could read the ticket and decide that a lookup would help. Both systems use the same tool. Only the second gives the model that choice. Likewise, the pipeline calls the model three times in a fixed order, while the router gives it a decision on a single call.

Now follow the money. The model proposes refunding the \$79 blender. The runtime checks the price and purchase date before it calls the refund handler. Choosing which order to refund and having permission to issue the refund are two separate decisions.

The same division applies at the end. The model can say the work is done. The runtime can ask for a receipt before accepting that claim, or end the run itself if time or money runs out.

To find the control boundary in another system, trace one actual request. What did the model see? Which step did it choose? What did the software allow, and what happened? ReAct illustrates how an observation from one action can inform the model’s reasoning about the next [@yao2023react].

## 2. Agency, autonomy, and consequences

In the blender case, the model chose to look up the orders and then proposed a refund for the matching one. That tells us something about its **agency**. The \$100 limit tells us when a person must step in. To understand the design, ask three questions.

| Dimension | Question to ask |
|---|---|
| **Agency and control** | Which choices can the model make? When can it choose again, and what new evidence can it use? |
| **Oversight and governance** | Which actions can go ahead automatically? Who approves the others? |
| **Risk and consequences** | What could an action change, who could be affected, and could the change be undone? |

**Autonomy** describes how independently the model can exercise its choices. A research agent might spend an hour choosing papers to read without asking anyone for approval. A payment system might give the model just one choice about where to send money. That one choice could have the greater consequence.

A coding agent makes the distinction concrete. It might choose tests and revise a patch on its own inside a temporary workspace. The runtime can still require a person’s approval before the patch reaches the shared repository.

When reviewing a design, identify who can widen those permissions and what happens when the model asks to do something beyond them.

## 3. One turn of the runtime {#concepts}

AutoResearch faces the same kind of choice as the support agent. It has a goal, a limited budget, and a result that may change its next move. Here the goal is to find training settings with a higher validation score before the computing budget runs out. The numbers in the figures are illustrative.

**Agent = Policy + State + Action Space + Environment Interface + Control Loop + Objective**

[]{#agent-control-animation}Watch job #42 in the next figure. When does the model first have enough evidence to suggest repeating the experiment? Follow the request from the controller, which keeps the run record, through the permission check to the executor, which sends it to the scheduler.

::: {#fig-agent-runtime}

```{=html}

{{< include _figures/runtime.html >}}

```

The learned policy proposes an operation. The runtime authorizes and dispatches the request. The scheduler applies it, and results return to inform the next decision.

:::

::: {#agent-control-transcript}
**Text walkthrough.** The starting score is 0.842. With two GPU-hours available, the model proposes a trial with learning rate 0.0003 and random seed 7. The runtime approves those exact settings and submits the request. The scheduler accepts it as job #42. At this point the runtime knows the job was accepted. Its score will arrive later.

Job #42 scores 0.851 and uses 0.6 GPU-hours. The runtime records the result, marks the job complete, and updates the remaining budget to 1.4 GPU-hours. The candidate is now the **incumbent**, the best configuration seen so far on validation. The model suggests repeating it with seed 11 to see whether the gain holds. The figure ends at that suggestion.
:::

**Policy.** The model uses the information it receives to propose a next step, such as repeating job #42. What it can propose depends on the choices and feedback the interface gives it. SWE-agent showed how changing that interface affected the way models navigated and edited code on the tasks studied [@yang2024sweagent].

**State and context.** Job #42 can finish before the runtime hears about it. The scheduler knows the job’s actual status. The runtime keeps its own record, called the **ledger**, with job IDs, results, and remaining budget. The **context** is the part the model sees on this turn. It might see a one-line summary even when the ledger holds the full history.

**Actions and observations.** The model can propose submitting a trial, waiting, or stopping. Those choices form its **action space**. When the runtime submits a job, the training service may return a job ID immediately and a score much later. Each returned piece of evidence is an **observation**.

::: {.callout-important}
## A proposal is separate from execution

Suppose the training service supports cancelling jobs. Is cancellation available on this turn? Does this run have permission to cancel job #42? Did the scheduler actually cancel it? Each question needs its own answer.
:::

The service lists supported operations in its **tool catalog**. The runtime exposes some of them to the model and checks permission for each specific request. Even after approval, the scheduler could report that the job had already finished. Its reply tells the runtime what happened. [Tool Use](03-tool-use.qmd) examines these checks in detail.

**Loop and objective.** After each result, the controller updates the ledger and decides whether to ask for another proposal. The objective gives those decisions a purpose. Here, a better validation score matters only if the search stays within budget.

## 4. A formal model of the turn

The equations describe one turn we've already seen in @fig-agent-control-progression. Read $t$ as “this turn” and $t+1$ as “the next turn.” Start with three events:

- The model proposes “refund order #1043.” That proposal is $\tilde a_t$.
- The runtime checks the order against the refund rule. The check is $\Gamma$ and its decision is $v_t$.
- The payment system issues the refund. The action it actually takes is $u_t$. The receipt is evidence the runtime can use on the next turn, $o_{t+1}$.

The same symbols work for AutoResearch. The goal $g$ is to improve the score within budget. Whether job #42 has finished is part of the world state $x_t$. The latest report the runtime has received is its observation $o_t$. Its ledger is $z_t$.

The next three lines show how the runtime prepares the input, gets a proposal, and checks permission.

$$
\begin{aligned}
c_t &= \phi(g,z_t,o_t) \\
\tilde a_t &\sim \pi_\theta(\cdot\mid c_t,\mathcal A_t^{\mathrm{avail}}) \\
v_t &= \Gamma(\tilde a_t,z_t,\mathcal A_t^{\mathrm{auth}},\rho_t)
\end{aligned}
$$

1. **Prepare.** $\phi$ combines the goal, the ledger, and the latest report into the context $c_t$ that the model sees.
2. **Propose.** The policy $\pi_\theta$ uses that context to propose one of the choices available on this turn, $\mathcal A_t^{\mathrm{avail}}$.
3. **Check.** The gate $\Gamma$ checks the proposal against the permitted operations $\mathcal A_t^{\mathrm{auth}}$ and current conditions $\rho_t$, such as budget or human approval. It can approve the exact request $a_t^{\mathrm{auth}}$, reject it, or pause for review.

Even after approval, the runtime may have an incomplete record. Suppose the scheduler starts job #42 but its reply gets lost. The job started ($u_t$), yet the runtime sees a timeout. Before retrying, it can check with the scheduler or reuse a request ID that the scheduler recognizes as a duplicate. If two jobs can spend the same budget, the service must also check the balance when it reserves the computing time.

The next four lines follow what happens after the request. The world changes, evidence may arrive, the runtime updates its record, and it decides whether to continue.

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{t+1} &\sim P(\cdot\mid x_t,u_t) \\
o_{t+1} &\sim O(\cdot\mid x_{t+1},u_t) \\
z_{t+1} &= U(z_t,\tilde a_t,e_t,o_{t+1}) \\
d_{t+1} &= D(g,z_{t+1},o_{t+1})
\end{aligned}
$$

The first two lines describe the world. $P$ describes how it changes, including changes outside the runtime. $O$ describes what evidence comes back. A job can finish while its score is still on the way.

The last two lines describe the runtime. $U$ updates the ledger using the proposal, the execution record $e_t$, and any new observation. The record can say “timed out” even when the outcome is still unknown.

$D$ decides whether to continue. Record why the run ended. A deadline can end a run while work is still unfinished. A hard stop prevents the model from taking another turn. The executor still has to account for jobs already running.

## 5. The RL, MDP, and POMDP connection

Suppose job #42 has finished, but the scheduler’s latest report still says “running.” Should AutoResearch wait, check again, or start a new trial? Reinforcement learning (RL) gives us a vocabulary for decisions like this. The table connects the names used in the lesson with their counterparts in sequential decision models [@sutton2018reinforcement].

| Agent engineering | RL or control abstraction |
|---|---|
| External system | Environment or plant |
| Latent world state $x_t$ | State governing transitions |
| Tool result, API response, or measurement $o_t$ | Observation |
| Proposal policy $\pi_\theta$ | Chooses a candidate operation from its inputs |
| Policy plus runtime | Effective policy at the environment boundary |
| Applied environment operation $u_t$ | Action in the environment model |
| Runtime state $z_t$ | Controller or information state |
| Model-visible context $c_t$ | Input to the proposal policy |
| Task objective and constraints | Criterion over trajectories |
| Runtime stopping rule | Rule for ending the run from controller information |

In a **Markov decision process (MDP)**, the current state contains the information needed to describe the chances of each next state and reward for a given action. With full observation, the decision maker sees that state. In a **partially observable MDP (POMDP)**, it sees clues. A delayed job report is one such clue. Checking again can prevent AutoResearch from starting a duplicate trial.

How confident should the controller be that the job has finished? In a discrete-state POMDP, a **belief** assigns a probability to each possible state. Given a starting distribution and models of how states change and observations arise, the controller can update those probabilities as evidence arrives [@kaelbling1998pomdp].

$$
b_t(x) = \mathbb P(x_t=x \mid o_{\le t},u_{<t}).
$$

Read $b_t(x)$ as “the probability that the world is in state $x$, given what we have seen and the actions that took effect.” That last part matters for a lost reply. If the runtime is unsure whether the job started, it must allow for both possibilities.

In practice, a summary of recent jobs can help the model choose its next action. Treating that summary as an **approximate information state** leaves open how much relevant history it captures and how reliable its estimates are. [Block 02](02-agent-loop-state-machines.qmd) develops controller state. [Block 04](04-context-state-memory.qmd) explains which evidence to keep.

One score can play several roles. When job #42 beats the baseline, AutoResearch can keep its settings for the next comparison. Whether the whole search succeeded is a later question. Read the table by asking what decision each quantity supports.

| Criterion | Example in an experiment agent |
|---|---|
| **Task objective** | Find better training settings within the computing budget. |
| **Promotion rule** | A candidate becomes the incumbent only if it strictly beats the incumbent on the validation metric and passes the protocol's artifact checks. |
| **Run success criterion** | The frozen final selection improves on the baseline when both are scored on the holdout. |
| **RL reward** | A scalar signal used to define return when the task is formulated as an RL problem. |
| **Model training loss** | The optimization objective used to fit the proposal model, such as token prediction loss. |
| **Evaluation metric** | Independently measured quality, cost, or completion for comparing deployed systems. |
| **Termination rule** | End when the trial cap, deadline, cancellation, or verified completion condition is reached. |

AutoResearch may use job #42’s score to pick a new trial while the model’s weights stay the same. It adapts during the run by reading results. Training the policy itself is a separate process covered in [Block 13](13-learning-agents-rl.qmd).

## 6. When a fixed workflow is the better design

Return to the cracked blender. What if the developer simply added a lookup whenever a ticket lacked an order number? Code could refund an order when exactly one item matched and it passed the \$100 and 30-day rule. Otherwise it could send the case to a person. This version would refund #1043 with one model call. Compare that outcome with the agent in @fig-agent-control-progression.

- **Clear rules.** If the business already knows how to make the decision, write the rule in code. The model can still extract the item name from the ticket.
- **Time and cost.** Each extra lookup or model call can make the customer wait. Measure the whole task, including retries and staff time.
- **Repeatability.** A fixed sequence makes a decision easier to reproduce. For an adaptive sequence, record which results, rules, and model version led to each choice.
- **Consequences of a mistake.** If two orders both match “blender,” an incorrect refund costs money. Passing an uncertain case to a person is one option to compare.

The agent has a stronger case when the customer’s wording is ambiguous and judgment helps resolve it. A team could route just those tickets to the agent. Compare the time saved with the extra calls, waiting time, and cost of mistakes. Anthropic’s design guidance also recommends starting with a simple approach [@anthropic2024effectiveagents].

A rule or a conventional optimizer can use feedback too. If one already works well, include it in the comparison. That helps isolate the value of the model’s judgment.

## 7. Production implications

Suppose a person approves one AutoResearch trial at a particular cost. The executor should check the approved settings, job identity, and compute reservation before submitting it. A change to those settings may need fresh approval. OpenAI’s guide describes human review for actions with significant consequences [@openaindbuildingagents].

If a trial seems to have run twice, you need to know where the second request came from. Record what the model proposed, what the runtime approved, what the executor sent, and what the scheduler confirmed. Count both attempts when measuring cost. Cancelling a job can prevent future spending, but earlier work still counts. [Reliability and Failure Recovery](10-reliability-recovery.qmd) covers missing replies and retries.

## 8. Building AutoResearch: the top-level design

Now put the pieces together. AutoResearch has a fixed computing budget and a starting configuration to beat. Every trial uses the same evaluator and validation metric. A separate **holdout** is data reserved for the final comparison, after the search has chosen its best settings. The [case study](../case-studies/autoresearch.qmd) connects this illustrative design to Karpathy’s training loop and the course’s local experiment [@karpathy2026autoresearch].

### Fixed or adaptive experiment selection
Both searches below get three trials. As you follow the first result, ask whether it can change what runs second.

::: {#fig-agent-experiment-control}

```{=html}

{{< include _figures/experiment-control.html >}}

```

In the fixed batch, scores determine the winner. In the adaptive loop, scores also affect which experiment runs next.

:::

In the fixed batch, someone chooses all three configurations before any scores arrive. The scores pick the winner. Trial selection is **open-loop** because an early score cannot change the schedule.

In the adaptive search, the first score can change which configuration runs second. That makes trial selection **closed-loop** even with a fixed limit of three trials. Either a conventional optimizer or a model can choose the next trial this way (@fig-agent-experiment-control).

### A high-level AutoResearch design

Follow the best configuration through @fig-autoresearch-design. When can it become the new incumbent, and when does AutoResearch first use the holdout? One controller manages this search. Later blocks consider splitting the work across roles.

::: {#fig-autoresearch-design}

```{=html}

{{< include _figures/autoresearch-design.html >}}

```

AutoResearch control loop. Follow Continue back to context building with the updated ledger, or Stop out to the final holdout evaluation.

:::

Job #42 from @fig-agent-runtime earns 0.851, above the starting score of 0.842. Once the runtime verifies and records the result, it makes these settings the incumbent. The run has used one of five trials and 0.6 of its two GPU-hours, so the model gets another turn. It suggests seed 11 to see whether the gain repeats.

When the runtime accepts a stop or reaches a limit, it freezes the selected configuration. Only then does it compare that configuration with the baseline on the holdout. The holdout score never guides another trial.

### Design decisions {#interview-system-design-mental-model}

**What should the agent beat?** Run a fixed batch with the same evaluator and computing budget. Then compare with a conventional optimizer that can also change its next trial after a result.

**Who chooses and who checks?** Let the model choose which settings to try next. The runtime checks permission and budget, records the result against the correct job ID, and applies the rule for replacing the incumbent.

**Is it worth deploying?** Give the alternatives the same budget and evidence. When comparing models that choose trials, keep their tools and inputs comparable. Check the final holdout result alongside computing cost, elapsed time, and human effort. [Agent Evaluation](09-agent-evaluation.qmd) develops this comparison.

**Empirical evidence.** MLAgentBench evaluates language agents on iterative ML experimentation [@huang2024mlagentbench]. MLE-bench compares model and scaffold combinations on offline Kaggle tasks [@chan2025mlebench]. Both illustrate evaluation under a specified protocol.

::: {.callout-tip}
## AutoResearch after Block 01

**Built in this block.** The protocol and ownership map, drawn as the top-level design in @fig-autoresearch-design.

- **Protocol.** Fix the baseline, evaluator, and validation metric before the first trial. Promote a candidate when it passes the artifact checks and strictly improves on the incumbent’s validation score. Set limits on trials and compute. Reserve the holdout for the final comparison.
- **Ownership.** The model proposes a trial or asks to stop. The runtime approves and submits trials, records the evaluator’s scores, selects the incumbent, and enforces the stopping rules.

**Next.** [Block 02](02-agent-loop-state-machines.qmd) gives the controller explicit states and shows how it can recover when a result goes missing.
:::

## 9. Conclusion

Return to the opening question. The customer left out the order number. A router can choose a handler from the ticket alone. The agent can ask for the orders, see which one contains the blender, and then choose what to propose. It gets a second decision with better information.

The same pattern appears in AutoResearch. The model can suggest another seed because it saw a promising score. The runtime checks whether that trial may run, records what happened, and decides whether the search can continue.

## 10. Companion reading {#companion-reading}

- *AI Agents in Action*, second edition, chapter 1, "The rise of AI agents," especially §1.1.1. Compare the chapter's assistant and autonomous agent patterns by the decisions each delegates [@lanham2026aiagents].
- *Building Applications with AI Agents*, chapter 1, "Introduction to Agents," especially "Workflows and Agents." Compare the book's terminology with the control boundary used here [@albada2025applications].

## 11. Conceptual questions

1. A router chooses Refund, but the order number is missing. This time the runtime shows the failure to the model, which then chooses Escalate. What new decision did the model get? What limits should the runtime enforce?

   <details class="agent-model-answer">
   <summary>Model answer</summary>

   The failure gave the model new information and a second choice. It now influences a short sequence of steps. Whether you call it an agent depends on your definition. The runtime should limit retries, check every refund proposal, and record the failed attempts.

   </details>

2. AutoResearch runs exactly five trials. The model sees each score and chooses the next settings. Which decisions belong to the model, and which belong to the runtime?

   <details class="agent-model-answer">
   <summary>Model answer</summary>

   Trial two’s score can change the model’s choice for trial three. That makes trial selection closed-loop. The runtime fixes the trial count, allowed operations, evaluation rules, and stopping point. Individual training scores may still vary.

   </details>

3. A coding agent is trying to fix a failing test. What can it choose, what can it observe, what does the runtime need to remember, and what would end the run?

   <details class="agent-model-answer">
   <summary>Model answer</summary>

   For a coding agent asked to fix a failing test, the **policy** may use a failed assertion to choose which supporting file to inspect next. Its **action space** might include reading an allowed file, proposing a patch, or running an allowlisted test. **Observations** include returned file contents, patch results, test output, and tool errors. The **environment** is the workspace, filesystem, and test runner. **Runtime state** records the task, workspace revision, edits and checks already attempted, pending operations, and remaining budget. The **terminal condition** can be verified success on the required checks, a resource limit, cancellation, or escalation. The task's acceptance checks determine success. A passing test is one possible piece of that evidence.

   </details>

4. A system can call tools but has no persistent memory beyond the context supplied to the current model call. Can it still be an agent? Is persistent memory necessary for agency?

   <details class="agent-model-answer">
   <summary>Model answer</summary>

   Yes. The current prompt can include the goal and latest tool result. That can be enough to choose a next step. A task that depends on older evidence needs some way to retrieve it. A run that must survive a restart also needs a durable record.

   </details>

5. Suppose, with hypothetical numbers, that a deterministic workflow succeeds 96% of the time, costs \$0.02, and takes 500 ms. An agent succeeds 97.5% of the time, costs \$0.40, and takes 14 seconds. What additional information would you need before deciding which system is better?

   <details class="agent-model-answer">
   <summary>Model answer</summary>

   Compare the two systems on the same representative tickets. Which cases account for the 1.5 percentage-point gain, and how certain is that estimate? Check how costly the failures are and how long the slowest customers wait. Include retries and human review in the cost. If you would send only difficult cases to the agent, explain how you would recognize them and include the cost of making that decision.

   </details>
